## Abstract

Estimating the durability of immunity from vaccination is complicated by unreported re-

vaccination, and unobserved natural infection or reexposure, which could result in

overestimation of protection longevity. We tested serial cross-sectional serum samples from

2005 to 2015 (N=2,530) for IgG to examine measles seroprevalence, spatiotemporal patterns of

titers across regions and antibody dynamics among children aged 1-9 years who grew up during

varying measles circulation in Madagascar under a one-dose vaccination schedule. We found

that measles seroprevalence has generally decreased over this time period. Furthermore, we

conducted two nested serological surveys, analyzing 393 samples taken in 2005 (N=158), a

time-point preceded by high levels of measles circulation, and 2015 (N=235), a time-point

preceded by low levels of measles circulation. Among children alive during periods of limited

measles circulation, we found lower measles seroprevalence in all age groups and lower

antibody titers in children aged 7-9 years old. Notably, titers among children aged 7-9 dipped

near the threshold of protection, highlighting the importance of additional measles vaccine

doses. Our findings suggest that vulnerabilities might emerge during periods of limited measles

circulation for countries with a one-dose schedule due to both the build-up of susceptible

individuals and waning titers.

## Introduction

Large-scale vaccine deployment beginning in the 20th century has prevented millions of

deaths around the globe(1). Prior to the introduction of vaccination, the immune landscape was

solely shaped by natural immunity where all individuals who had antibodies against a specific

pathogen acquired them either through natural infection or through maternal immunity which

quickly wanes. Expanding vaccination opportunities limits pathogen circulation meaning that an

accelerating number of individuals acquire vaccinal immunity (e.g., vaccine-induced antibodies)

rather than natural immunity. Although acquiring immunity via vaccination rather than disease-

causing infection is preferred, the switch may mean that individuals have less durable protection

as a result of both lower overall titers if vaccines are less immunogenic(2) and less opportunity

for boosting of titers by re-exposure. These possibilities remain poorly characterized, yet

defining differences in the dynamics of naturally-acquired antibodies and vaccine-acquired

antibodies in different landscapes of infection exposure could help anticipate future disease risk,

and inform necessary vaccination schedule updates.

The recent re-emergence of some vaccine-preventable diseases (VPDs) in areas with

high vaccination coverage provides evidence that vaccinal immunity may wane in the absence

of immunity-boosting events from natural infection(3–7). Waning vaccinal immunity contributed

to recent mumps outbreaks(3,8) and age-structured models have shown that accounting for re-

exposure and immune boosting is required to explain pertussis dynamics and reemergence in

areas with high vaccine coverage(6,7). As disease incidence declines, a growing number of

children and adults will never have had natural exposure to VPDs (either infection or boosting).

Therefore, protective vaccinal immunity may wane more quickly, leading to outbreaks among

vaccinated individuals, and a shift in age-specific incidence to older individuals who have lost

their vaccine-induced antibodies(3,7). Periods of limited or no natural circulation provide a

useful stress test of vaccinal immunity durability, generating evidence of the consequences of

the absence of re-exposure and subsequent boosting events(3,6).

Measles is a highly contagious VPD which transmits via direct contact or through

airborne particles(9). Measles remains a serious public health burden globally(10) despite

vaccine introduction in 1963 and vast subsequent expansion of vaccination coverage and

surveillance. Measles outbreaks are largely concentrated among unvaccinated groups, with a

few exceptions (11–16) and measles vaccine and natural immunity is known to be robust, with

antibody mediated protections lasting >25 years (with some variation shaped by number and

timing of vaccinations, vaccine strains, exposure history and subsequent boosting events as

well as human genetic heterogeneities(17–22)). Indeed, the measles vaccine has been shown

to be slightly less immunogenic than immunity from natural infection as antibody titers following

vaccination are lower than natural infection but still above the threshold of seroprotection(2,23–

27). A recent study conducted in the United States found that 10% of participants who received

3 measles doses were seronegative 9-11 years after vaccination(28). A multi-dose vaccine

schedule and durable antibody response(18,28,29) may be essential to lifelong protection, and

it remains unclear whether re-emergence of measles among vaccinated individuals is of

concern for settings where only one dose is administered. These characteristics make measles

a prime candidate to assess how its immune landscape is impacted in the absence of natural

circulation and boosting events particularly in a setting where only one dose of the measles

vaccine is administered.

Madagascar's recent measles history provides the opportunity to probe the implications

of a changing immune landscape with a one-dose schedule, as the country recently

experienced its first period of extremely reduced measles circulation after the introduction of

vaccination in 1985 (30) (Fig. 1). Although the number of measles cases decreased dramatically

following vaccine introduction, circulation persisted until 2004 (Fig. 1). Between 2006 and 2017

only a handful of measles cases were reported (Fig. S1). This was followed by a large outbreak

between 2018 and 2020, a result of longstanding low vaccination coverage and suboptimal

supplementary immunization activities (SIA) (31,32) (Fig. 1, Table S1). The 2018 measles

outbreak had over 100,000 reported cases across all 22 regions with a mean age of infection of

9 years and faster growth in regions with higher vaccination coverage(31,33). In 2016, a

measles cross-sectional serological survey (serosurvey) had highlighted the potential for a

measles outbreak given that measles susceptibility was over 10% across the population(34).

Cross-sectional serosurveys in Madagascar for poliovirus, pertussis, diphtheria and measles

have assessed age-specific seroprotection and vaccination coverage but longitudinal studies

probing antibody dynamics across different disease landscapes are lacking due to high costs

and difficulty in sample collection and testing(34–37).

In lieu of a longitudinal serosurvey which is costly and difficult to perform, we leveraged

11 years of routinely collected serum samples (2005-2015) to examine measles

seroprevalence, spatial patterns of antibody titers and antibody dynamics across periods of

collection. We explored the spatiotemporal patterns of measles antibody titers across

Madagascar’s regions, given known differences in vaccination coverage, to uncover how the

immune landscape (i.e., the distribution of antibody titers) might evolve as the measles infection

landscape shifts. Lastly, we established two nested serosurveys, selecting samples collected in

either 2005 or 2015, to examine measles seroprevalence and antibody dynamics across periods

of varying measles circulation (Fig. 2).

## Methods

Sample selection

We used serum samples from Madagascar’s febrile-rash surveillance system which

collects a patient’s serum whenever they present for care with measles-like symptoms at any

health facility across the country. These serum samples are tested for measles-specific and

rubella-specific immunoglobulin M (IgM) antibodies at the Institut Pasteur de Madagascar and

any leftover serum is stored(34). A previous study tested 4,465 samples collected between

November 2004 and December 2015 for measles immunoglobulin G (IgG) antibody titers with

an indirect ELISA test (Enzygnost Anti-Measles Virus/IgG; Siemens, Erlangen, Germany) with a

sensitivity of 90% and a specificity of 100%(34,39). Quantitative titers were evaluated using the

alpha method outlined in kit insert with an upper limit of 10,000 milli-international units per

milliliter (mIU/mL).

To obtain a wide range of individuals who experienced different measles circulation

conditions, we considered all 4,465 samples tested by Winter et al., 2018 (previous work

focused on samples collected after October 2013) (33,34). We excluded samples which were

not stored at the proper temperature, samples lacking storage temperature information and

samples with no information on an individual’s age. We also removed samples which tested

positive or equivocal for measles IgM antibodies (N=42) indicative of a recent measles infection

or vaccination, as these individuals are in the process of establishing their measles IgG

antibodies and would bias analyses of quantitative IgG titers. We excluded the 29 samples

collected in 2004 as we only had samples collected from 2 months of the year resulting in a

lower sample size compared to 2005-2015 from which samples were collected year-round.

Earlier years had fewer samples available as the surveillance system was ramping up and more

health centers started to participate in sample collection. We focused all of our analyses on

children between 1 and 9 years old at the time of sampling. A total of 2,530 samples across

various ages and regions were selected to assess trends in measles IgG seroprevalence and

antibody titers across different sampling years and regions (Fig. S2, Tables S2-S3).

Initially, we calculated yearly measles seroprevalence and geometric mean titers (GMT)

from 2005 to 2015. All individuals with measles IgG titers ≥ 331 mIU/mL were classified as

seropositive by the manufacturer’s standards. Individuals with titers < 150 mIU/mL were

classified as seronegative. We fit a generalized additive model (GAM) with year of sample

collection as a predictor of an individuals’ binary serostatus (0=seronegative; 1=seropositive) to

assess non-linear patterns across the 11 year period. Individuals with titers ≥ 150 mIU/mL and <

331 mIU/mL were classified as equivocal and were excluded for this analysis. Geometric mean

titers were calculated for each year by taking the anti-log of the mean of the log antibody

concentration for all non-zero titers. All geometric and arithmetic mean titer calculations

excluded titers from seronegative individuals. The mgcv R package was used to fit all

GAMs(40,41).

Spatiotemporal patterns of measles antibody titers and vaccination coverage

Next, we explored how measles titers varied across regions of varying vaccination

levels, and by exposure probability (i.e., individuals who had and had not been alive during

periods of measles circulation). Since reliable measles vaccination coverage is not available at

the regional level, we estimated measles vaccination coverage from the Demographic Health

Survey (DHS) collected in 2008/2009 which reported measles vaccination status for children

under 5 years old (42). The DHS is a nationally representative household survey conducted

across Madagascar which collected information on vaccination status for children under 5 at the

time of the survey as reported by a parent or the presence of a vaccination card. This was the

only DHS conducted between 2005 and 2015 which reported measles vaccination status along

with an individual’s region. In this analysis, children were considered to be vaccinated if

vaccination was reported by their mother or indicated by a vaccination card, an approach used

previously by other researchers(43). It is possible that children were vaccinated by either routine

on schedule vaccination or by an SIA or by both thus vaccination coverage estimates are an

accumulation of all vaccination efforts. We calculated region specific measles vaccination

coverage for children aged 9 to 59 months old (N=9,747). Since measles vaccine eligibility

starts at 9 months, we excluded all children under 9 months old at the time of the survey from

our vaccination coverage estimates. Then, GMTs were calculated for each region using all

positive and equivocal samples collected from 2005 to 2015 and broken down by individuals

who were alive during periods of high measles circulation (i.e., born prior to 2006) (N=971) and

by individuals alive during periods of low natural measles circulation (i.e., born after 2006)

(N=1,099). We used a linear regression weighted by sample size to assess the relationship

between the region's estimated measles vaccine coverage and geometric mean titer.

Nested serosurvey sample selection

To establish two cohorts that experienced different levels of measles circulation, we

conducted two nested serosurveys within our 2,530 samples. We selected all samples collected

in either 2005 or 2015. Individuals in the 2005 nested serosurvey (N=158) were alive during

periods of frequent measles outbreaks in Madagascar while individuals in the 2015 serosurvey

(N=235) have never experienced a measles outbreak (Fig. 2). Reported measles cases varied

between zero and six between 2006 and 2015 indicating a very small probability that individuals

in our 2015 serosurvey were naturally exposed to measles. Given the measles surveillance

system in Madagascar and measles’ extremely high R0, it is not likely that there were outbreaks

that went undetected between 2006 and 2015. We assumed that the children sampled within

Madagascar also grew up in Madagascar and were not exposed to measles in other countries.

To compare seroprevalence across the two serosurvey years, we first used a chi-

squared test to test for overall differences, and then fit a GAM to explore trends across ages.

Individuals with equivocal measles IgG status were removed for the chi-squared test and the

GAM. Then we explored quantitative difference in titers by calculating GMT along with 95%

confidence interval for each nested serosurvey across ages. In addition to GMT, we also tested

for a difference between arithmetic mean titers across ages in the two serosurvey years using a

student’s t-test and fit a GAM to explore trends in measles IgG titers across age. To explore

impacts at later ages, we expanded the 2005 nested serosurvey to include individuals aged 1 to

14 (N=197) at the time of sampling to examine antibody trends and fit a GAM for individuals

who were classified as seropositive or equivocal (N=187). We were unable to expand the 2015

## Results

Initially, we examined measles seroprevalence and titers among the 2,530 samples

collected between 2005 and 2015 in Madagascar (Fig. 3). The proportion of children with

measles IgG titers above the threshold of seroprotection (≥ 331 mIU/mL) decreased from 92.5%

in 2005 to 74.6% in 2015 (Fig. 3). This decline was also observed when we fit a generalized

additive model with year of sample collection as a predictor of an individual’s binary serostatus

(Fig. S3). Measles GMT trended downward from 1,702 mIU/mL in 2005 to 1,202 mIU/mL in

2015 (Fig. 3 red line) but remained above 331 mIU/mL, the threshold of seroprotection.

Inferences at this scale are complicated by various epidemiological and immunological variables

like age at sampling, vaccination status and infection history which all contribute to the observed

titer.

Next, we used the 2008/2009 DHS data to map vaccination coverage by region and

show that measles vaccination was higher around the capital, Antananarivo (located near the

center of the country) and lower in the periphery (Fig. S4A). Lower titers were observed in the

center of the country, with higher titers in other regions when looking at titers from individuals

who have been alive during periods of high measles circulation (i.e., born prior to 2006) (Figs.

S4B and S5A). Overall, regions with higher vaccination coverage exhibited lower measles titers

across individuals alive during periods of high measles circulation (P<0.05) (Fig. S4C). Regional

titer differences were less apparent when looking at individuals who have been alive during

periods of low measles circulation (i.e., born after 2006) since this immune landscape is

composed mostly of vaccinal immunity (Figs. S4D and S5B). Regions with higher vaccination

coverage exhibited slightly lower measles titers (P<0.05) but the slope was shallower (-16.8

mIU/mL vs. -9.16 mIU/mL) indicating a weaker relationship between vaccination coverage and

GMT (Fig. S4C and S4D).

Our nested serosurveys in 2005 and 2015 allowed us to examine seroprevalence and

antibody dynamics at a finer scale while accounting for age at sampling and epidemiological

variables (e.g., shared infection and vaccination probability) (Fig. S6 and Table S4). Children

included in the 2005 serosurvey grew up during periods of yearly measles circulation with

showed that lower measles seroprevalence among the children in the 2015 serosurvey was

more evident in children aged three to six (Fig. S7).

Additionally, we found similar titers among children 1 to 6 years of age across both

serosurveys but titers in children aged 7 to 9 were significantly lower in children sampled in the

2015 serosurvey (Figs. 4B and S8). This pattern remained consistent across geometric mean

(Fig. 4B) and arithmetic mean (Fig. S8A) calculations. A generalized additive model fit to the

individual level data yielded the same results (Fig. S8B). At age 9, children in the 2005

serosurvey had GMT of 2,818 mIU/mL (confidence interval (CI): 1,660-4,677 mIU/mL) while

children in the 2015 serosurvey had GMT of 630 mIU/mL (417-977 mIU/mL) (Fig. 4B). We

extended the 2005 serosurvey to include children between the ages of 10 and 14 and found that

titers continued to increase for children growing up in periods of measles circulation (Fig. S9).

## Discussion

To understand future disease risk requires understanding differences in dynamics of

naturally-acquired antibodies and vaccine-acquired antibodies as incidence of VPDs changes.

We leveraged a unique 11-year cross-sectional measles antibody dataset to examine measles

seroprevalence, antibody dynamics and spatial patterns across periods of varying measles

incidence to characterize antibody titers in diverse epidemiological settings. The 2,530 samples

collected from children between 1 and 9 years of age from 2005 to 2015 in Madagascar indicate

that measles seroprevalence has generally decreased over this period (Figs. 2 and S3). This is

likely attributed to individuals who are not vaccinated and the subsequent build-up of

susceptibles within the population in an era with no outbreaks.

We found that regions in central Madagascar with higher vaccination coverage had

lower measles titers compared to regions where vaccination coverage was lower (Fig. S4). This

11

relationship was stronger for individuals who were alive during periods of high measles

circulation. One explanation for this difference in immune landscapes is that regions with

historically lower vaccination coverage are likely to have more measles circulation which

induces a higher antibody titer than vaccination. Furthermore, previously vaccinated or infected

individuals in these regions might also be more likely to be boosted than individuals in regions

with higher vaccination coverage and lower circulation. Measles incidence by region in

Madagascar prior to 2006 was not available to pursue this further. At this scale, changes from a

landscape of immunity shaped by infection and vaccination to one solely shaped by vaccination

does not appear to be of great concern since titers are above the threshold of seropositivity.

However, it is difficult to make any definitive interpretations as the differences in titers could

ultimately be explained by differences in timing of vaccination and/or natural infection or due to

the skewed age distribution of the two groups (Fig. S6).

Our ability to make population level inferences using all of our samples is hindered by

the common limitations arising from convenience samples (e.g., small sample sizes, lack of

adequate regional and age representation and missing vaccination information) in addition to

hidden immunological heterogeneities arising from age at sampling and vaccination/infection

history. Since serum samples for this study were collected from individuals who presented for

medical care it is possible that this resulted in a nonrepresentative sample of the population. If

there is a relationship between health seeking behavior when individuals have febrile illness

with measles vaccination and/or infection incidence, then our seroprevalence and antibody level

estimates may not be an accurate representation of the population. In this study, we predict

resulting biases are likely to go in the opposite direction of the pattern we are exploring:

individuals who sought care for fever or rash at a healthcare facility and thus have access to a

healthcare facility are more likely to have been reached by a vaccination campaign than children

in more remote settings. Given this bias, we might expect that the seroprevalence estimates

among these convenience samples are higher than the true seroprevalence among all

individuals. The lower seroprevalence that we observe might in fact be even lower, raising

greater concern. Given these challenges, we then focused on characterizing trends within our

convenience samples without generalizing to the entire population. Accordingly, we conducted

two nested serosurveys which allowed us to control for some of the previously mentioned

limitations and address the question of measles seroprevalence and antibody dynamics across

varying levels of measles circulation.

Most notably, we found lower measles seroprevalence in children aged 1 to 9 and lower

antibody titers among children aged 7 to 9 in the 2015 serosurvey who were alive during periods

without ongoing measles circulation (Figs. 4, S7 and S8). The lower seroprevalence among the

individuals in the 2015 serosurvey is likely a result of missed vaccination and limited

seroconversion by natural measles exposure since there were no outbreaks (Figs. 4A and S7).

Higher seroprevalence in the 2005 nested serosurvey can be attributed to routine vaccination,

annual measles circulation and the 2004 catch up SIA which targeted children 9 months to 14

years old. The lower measles titers among children aged 7 to 9 in 2015 when compared to

children 7 to 9 in 2005 can also likely be attributed to waning of vaccine-acquired immunity

either due to the absence of boosting events from natural infection or subsequent vaccination

via SIA or less durable vaccine-acquired titers (Figs. 4B and S8). The trend that titers continue

to increase across age groups for individuals alive during periods of high measles circulation

remains evident when we extended the 2005 nested serosurvey to incorporate individuals up to

14 years of age (Fig. S9). This finding is supported by the idea that the fast-scale responses

elicited by short-lived plasma cells can mask more durable antibody titers and ultimately hide

dynamics produced by the long-lived plasma cells when boosting from subsequent exposure is

frequent(5). Frequent boosting experienced by individuals in the 2005 serosurvey who grew up

during measles circulation or who may have received an additional dose during the 2004 SIA

may have obscured the dynamics of the long-lived plasma cell produced antibodies which can

be seen in the 2015 serosurvey.

This inference assumes that individuals in each age group were vaccinated on schedule

and therefore have similar elapsed times since their vaccination which is not always the case. A

previous study found that 81% of vaccinated Malagasy children were vaccinated between 9 and

12 months of age(44). Here, we may be unable to detect the true waning signature due to off-

schedule vaccination or SIAs (Figs. 4B and S8), both of which could result in secondary

vaccination and thus boosting (Table S1). Both scenarios would skew the GMT to be higher

within each age group (Figs. 4B and S8). All individuals in the 2005 nested serosurvey were

eligible for 2004 SIA. In the 2015 nested serosurvey, individuals aged 2 to 4 years old were

eligible for the 2013 SIA, individuals aged 5 to 7 years old were eligible for both the 2010 and

2013 SIAs and individuals aged 8 and 9 years old were eligible for both the 2007 and 2010

SIAs. The SIAs in 2007 and 2013 targeted individuals aged 9 months to 59 months old while the

2010 SIA targeted individuals aged 9 months to 47 months old (Table S1). Our findings highlight

that it might be beneficial to expand age targets for follow up SIAs to align with the catch up

ORIGINAL UNEDITED MANUSCRIPT


<!-- Page 14 -->


13

SIAs targeting children up 14 years old to help increase seroprevalence and combat waning

vaccinal immunity (Fig. S9).

Our results align with previous work indicating lower titers during the vaccine era in

Luxembourg, where children aged 10 to 16 who lived in an area with circulating measles had

higher titers compared to children of the same age living in an area with no circulating

measles(45). Similarly, a study conducted in Tanzania among children aged 18 months to 5

years old found that measles antibody titers did not decrease significantly and hypothesized that

re-exposure to the measles virus in endemic areas might be part of the explanation(46).

The decline in geometric mean titer across age seen in the 2015 serosurvey is

concerning since titers in children over 7 appear to be approaching the threshold of

seropositivity, raising the question of whether these children will become seronegative in the

absence of boosting events from an additional measles vaccine dose (Fig. 4B). However, a

second measles vaccine dose was introduced in 2020 in Madagascar which should boost

existing titers and capture any individuals who missed the first dose. Interestingly, the mean age

of infection for the 2018 measles outbreak in Madagascar was 9 when typically, it has been 2-

5(33). A higher mean age of infection is a common characteristic of post-honeymoon outbreaks

due to the build-up of susceptibles who missed on-time vaccination and are now older. It is

unclear whether waning immunity among vaccinated Malagasy children might have contributed

to the pool of susceptibles that fueled the 2018 outbreak.

Although these results suggest that measles IgG titers in some individuals might fall

below the threshold for seropositivity in the absence of boosting and in the context of a single

vaccine dose, cellular immunity and measles-specific neutralizing antibodies might still be

present and offer protection against infection, especially since measles IgG titers decline faster

than measles-specific neutralizing antibodies(47,48). Vaccinated but seronegative individuals

are likely still protected from measles infection by their memory T cells(49). Researchers must

continue to explore the underlying immunological and epidemiological factors influencing

antibody dynamics specifically under varying exposure probabilities and a changing immune

landscape. Longitudinal studies of well characterized individuals with known vaccination

schedules and infection status in areas of varying transmission will provide crucial information to

probe these questions.

## Conclusion

Evidence of age-specific declines in mean titers during periods of limited measles

circulation in Madagascar highlights the importance of additional measles doses, currently the

global health target in most settings. Beyond immunizing seronegative individuals (at

considerable costs in terms of morbidity and mortality), measles circulation might also boost

pre-existing titers through exposures that do not lead to infection, preventing waning of vaccine-

acquired antibodies, leading to a different landscape of immune vulnerabilities. For measles,

vaccine acquired antibodies remain above the threshold for seroprotection even with a single

dose and in the absence of boosting. However, the degree to which this holds across VPDs is

unclear. Our findings reveal the value of analyzing titers quantitatively when conducting

serological surveillance especially when comparing different populations under different

epidemiological contexts of vaccination and natural circulation to illuminate antibody dynamics

and subsequent implications for disease control. Changing antibody dynamics under varying

exposure risks and vaccination schedules is a potentially important component of future

population vulnerability for measles but also other immunizing infections.

*Figure 1. Madagascar measles cases and vaccination coverage from 1980 to 2022. The annual number of reported measles cases (in thousands) is displayed by the gray bars. No data was available for 2005. Reported measles cases ranged from 0 to 11 between 2006 and 2017 and are not visible due to the scaling of the y-axis (See Fig. S1). Measles vaccine was introduced in 1985 and reported administrative coverage (black line) and the WHO/UNICEF estimated vaccination coverage (gray line) are plotted thereafter. A 2nd dose of the measles vaccine was introduced in 2020 and reported administrative coverage (red line) and the WHO/UNICEF estimated vaccination coverage (blue line) are plotted thereafter. Administrative coverage data is calculated by dividing the total number of doses distributed by the size of the target population in that region while the WHO/UNICEF estimated coverage predicts actual vaccines administered. Years where supplemental immunization activity (SIA) occurred are indicated by the green arrow (See Table S1). Data source: World Health Organization(30,38)*

*Figure 2. Madagascar measles cases and vaccination coverage experienced by each nested serosurvey group. The annual number of reported measles cases (in thousands) is displayed by the gray bars. Reported measles cases ranged from 0 to 6 between 2006 and 2015 and are not visible due to the scaling of the y-axis (See Fig. S1). Reported measles vaccine administrative coverage is displayed by the black line and the WHO/UNICEF estimated vaccination coverage by the gray line. Years where supplemental immunization activity (SIA) occurred are indicated by the green dashed line (See Table S1) and serosurvey sample collection is indicated by the dotted red line. A) Epidemiological context experienced by children sampled in the 2005 nested serosurvey. B) Epidemiological context experienced by children sampled in the 2015 nested serosurvey. Data source: World Health Organization*

*Figure 3. Yearly distribution of measles IgG antibody seroprevalence and geometric mean titer (GMT) among samples from Madagascar’s febrile-rash surveillance system (N=2,530). Black bars display the percentage of individuals whose serum was collected by Madagascar’s national fever rash surveillance system who were seropositive against measles (titers ≥ 331 mIU/mL) and between the ages of 1 and 9 years old at the time of collection. Light gray bars represent seronegative individuals (titers < 150 mIU/mL) and dark gray bars represent equivocal individuals (titers ≥ 150 mIU/mL and < 331 mIU/mL). Red line displays the geometric mean titer of all seropositive and equivocal individuals. The total number of samples collected in each year is displayed in the top row.*

*Figure 4. Age distribution of measles IgG seroprevalence and geometric mean titer from both nested serosurveys in Madagascar. A) Bars display the percentage of individuals whose serum was seropositive against measles (titers ≥ 331 mIU/mL) for each age group in years. The 2005 nested serosurvey is represented by the black bars while the 2015 nested serosurvey is represented by the gray bars. Total number of individuals in each age group is indicated at the top of each bar. B) Geometric mean titers are represented by the circle with 95% confidence intervals displayed by the lines. The 2005 nested serosurvey is represented by the black points and lines while the 2015 nested serosurvey is represented by the gray points and lines. Total number of individuals in each age group is indicated at the top. The red dashed line represents the threshold of seropositivity.*
